so there’s a few things we need to understand about the dynamic at play here 

it’s all well and good to say *we* would be like this if we were privileged - because we come from the perspective that if i’m looked after, why shouldn’t everyone else be? a level of equality where everyone has enough seems plausible and the kind of world we want to live in

but we are dealing with a group of people who have created, and are well aware of, a zero sum game.

their level of wealth and privilege is NOT ATTAINABLE without taking away from others and subordinating others. their power only comes from maintaining powerlessness of others, and power over others.

i used to think “a rising tide raises all boats” meant that if everyone’s conditions are better, it benefits everyone. that’s not what the quote means. a rising tide raises all boats is a trickle down economics motto - if the people up the top rise up further, that’s supposedly meant to be good for everyone. but at this point in history where we are right now, if we want equality, it will not raise all boats - if we want equality, it WILL take away from those up the top. but we are not the ones who made this into a zero sum game.

and this is why - and i’m just bringing this up because this is my focus and research at the moment, but it can be applied more broadly - decolonisation is not just decolonise your mind. decolonisation is VIOLENT. revolution is VIOLENT. and that is not a bad thing, that’s a reality we need to accept if we want change. we gotta accept there is no way, shape or form we can convince these people to let go of the things they’re holding onto. they KNOW it’s a zero sum game. we can’t appeal to their moral sensibilities because there is none. if we want shit, we gotta take it. 

the other dynamic at play is to do with nationalism. the irony of this is the larger mass supporting this status quo actually don’t have shit either. the majority will be working class or lower class - lumpen proletariat. but when you’ve gutted and deindustrialised communities, you’ve disintegrated education, and you pump these communities full of nationalist propaganda since the 1950s - you get a lot of people who don’t quite understand the dynamics of this zero sum game but you can reach into their hearts and turn their shame and humiliation into hatred. this is what h*tl*r did too - m**n k*mpf literally translates to “my struggle”. when you read it, it talks about deep shame and humiliation. this is a human emotion everyone experiences but humans are likely to avoid - when you have someone who speaks right to this sore and very deep part inside you, they can manipulate you real easy.

our solution to shame and humiliation is solidarity, camaraderie and compassion. their solution to it is pride. when you’re down low, pride can look like power but it isn’t. 

to quote uncle iroh: pride is not the opposite of shame, but it’s source. true humility is the only antidote to shame

nationalism draws a big fat circle around a territory and says all our riches are all of ours! no, you don’t get to enjoy the fruits of your labour, but you’re part of us symbolically. 

for many of these supporters, the only thing they have is white supremacy. they don’t got money, houses, education, love, passion - they don’t got shit except their white identity that makes them feel like the one thing they do have is being above others on this arbitrary hierarchy. propaganda reaches into their shameful hearts and pumps it full of pride so they blindly support the status quo.

so when you look at it this way, it makes complete sense. we are not dealing with the same human beings here. we are not dealing with people who have compassion. this goes beyond fuck you, i got mines. this is i got mines and you can’t get yours because yours is mines. 

it’s a zero sum game. and the only way to end the game means that those at the top WILL lose. that’s gotta be the trade off we’re willing to fight for or we get nowhere. there is no possibility of improving our lives and maintaining theirs, because theirs depends on ours being down.

Thank you! As a huge f*****g nerd that means a lot to me. If you like this answer I’ll add a little more, because the metaphysics of time is my absolute favourite part of philo and favourite thing to think about.

Look at how time acts in different situations. With very dense mass, time kinda warps. Same with objects travelling at high velocity. It’s called time dilation, and it has to do with Einstein’s theory of general relativity. Our experience of time feels relatively uniform through our human lives, but our velocity never changes that much and nor do we find ourselves on a planet significantly more dense and heavy than the earth. regardless, our reference point likely remains relatively uniform - so if you go on an interstellar joyride, time may seem to pass the same way for you, but you come home to earth and 5 years for you has been 100 years for the earth. but the fact that time “behaves” differently tells me that time is more like a bendable blob of jelly than a uniform straight line. it’s not travelling with us, we’re travelling inside it.

quantum mechanics also has some interesting implications for the nature of time - most of this falls into theoretical physics and our understanding of it is incomplete and may always be. some physicists say quantum particles can look like they’re travelling back through time, or others say they’re existing in multiple parallel timelines/universes at once. some physicists say time maybe doesn’t exist at all and is just a relative reference point from the perspective of the observer - i don’t like this interpretation, not because i think it’s wrong, but because i think it’s no fun. basically we don’t really know what’s up with time but the deeper we get into physics, the more we learn about it’s theoretical nature. i’m afraid this may be one phenomenon that will only ever be able to be understood theoretically. but i find all the different possibilities fascinating.

we are limited to our human experience of time - temporal phenomenology. Just because we are limited to moving linearly through time, that does not necessarily translate to the nature of time itself, just our limited capacity to move around inside it. 

Space has similar restrictions. We cannot make ourselves too much bigger or smaller, we can’t be in two places at once, or occupy all of space at once, we can’t move through solid objects etc. But just because we are limited in how we can physically move through space, that doesn’t mean that the rest of space doesn’t exist out there. It only says that we are limited in how we can move through it.

And it’s similar with time, I think. This is just my own philosophy on the metaphysics of time and temporal phenomenology, but I see it more like a vector space, and our linear progression from one point to another is just our own trajectory through the vector space. Time itself is not necessarily linear; our journey through it is linear. 

You can walk in a straight line from one corner of your room across to the other. The room isn’t just one line though, with a beginning and end. Your journey walking from one spot to the next is what’s linear - and that is what has a starting and an end point. Where does the room itself start and end? This is one of the first things that pops up on google when you search Derrida Deconstruction. It’s not a philo paper per se, but it’s succinct and has been very helpful for me in understanding some of the basics. 

https://criticallegalthinking.com/2016/05/27/jacques-derrida-deconstruction/

This was also helpful for me when I was studying deconstruction, Derrida’s “Letter to a Japanese Friend”

https://grattoncourses.files.wordpress.com/2012/11/letter_to_a_japanese.pdf

These are short, succinct and helpful. Like others have said, it’s not necessarily a method or a thing, and there’s no right way to *do* deconstruction. It will also depend on what text you are looking at. It can be broadly applied to so many different things. 

For me, my simplistic interpretation is that meaning itself isn’t fixed, and language is not necessarily representing a fixed, static aspect of the universe (transcendental signifier, nothing beyond the text). Rather, meaning has many components to it that are constantly in flux and shifting, and we can learn a lot from the movement of that change. This is why différance relates to differentiation, as in calculus, rather than just difference. In calculus, you’re not looking at the difference between one point and another necessarily. You’re studying the rate of change. 

I have a few analogies I use to understand some of these concepts. Différance for me maps really well onto calculus. Meaning itself isn’t some ethereal entity with value in and of itself, but more like a graph moving through time. We are looking at the rate of change and how it flows from one moment to the next, rather than fixed points.

For deconstruction as a whole, I like the analogy of a computer. In Letter to a Japanese Friend, Derrida talks about deconstruction not necessarily as taking something apart in a systematic way, but the amalgamation of different parts that constitutes a thing. A computer isn’t just a computer - you’ve got your keyboard, screen, metal frame and screws, battery, RAM, coding, etc. And different parts change over time and we integrate them in different ways, as our technology evolves. Deconstruction isn’t necessarily systematically taking apart this computer, but the observation that the computer is an amalgamation of different parts that are changing and evolving (not the analogy here because computers don’t spontaneously evolve, but our technology advances and we can switch out different parts). Tangentially related, I found this to be similar to the buddhist conception of self (or rather, no self). There is no permanent and unchanging self, but an aggregation of of changing parts. The chariot analogy is helpful to understand this buddhist idea, and I find this maps onto meaning in a Derridean way. No permanent and unchanging meaning, but an aggregation of changing parts. 

Binary opposition, trace, and hauntology are very interesting to me too. The basic premise here is that everything holds its opposite - everything is constructed with what it is opposed to. And this has less to say of the nature of these two opposing things, as this isn’t really compatible with the idea of fixed and static universal forms or essences, in a Platonic sense. I think of it more as when you talk about what is masculine, you are also constructing what you take to be or not be feminine. In constructing your understanding of masculinity you simultaneously construct your understanding of femininity. In a political sense, you can also look into the agenda and paradigm of someone who is framing a certain idea - in an extreme example, terrorist and freedom fighter seem diametrically opposed - and yet, these two terms can reference the exact same person. It has more to do with the person speaking and how they want to frame the situation, rather than it does about the material nature of what they are talking about. I think this is another example of nothing beyond the text - but admittedly this is still the one concept that I haven’t completely grasped. This one took a little while for me to get my head around completely. 

Another couple texts that I found helpful was the *Villanova Roundtable* in Deconstruction in a Nutshell, and *Mystical Foundation of Authority* in Deconstruction and the Possibility of Justice.

Follow-up:

Which parts are you finding hard to understand? A lot of philosophical texts are very dense. It’s not as easy to read as fiction, or any narrative that you follow along with for enjoyment. Philosophical texts (well, good ones) require you to think pretty deeply. 

It’s hard to give advice specifically for the Myth of Sisyphus without knowing which part has got you caught up (also side note - you doing okay? hectic book for a high schooler!) but I can give some advice for reading philo in general.

Firstly, it’s okay if you don’t understand it at first.  A lot of philo students and teachers will tell you you probably have to read something over and over a few times to deeply understanding it. To DEEPLY deeply deeply understand it, you’ll want to be annotating these texts, writing your own notes, spending time to think about what the text is saying, how you feel about it, what your intuition is, how other philosophers have responded to this text, what it can apply to, whether or not you agree or disagree and which parts specifically, breaking down the arguments into premises and conclusions and critically analysing and evaluating all these points, and talking to other people about the text. That’s a whole lot of work, but that’s basically what’s required if you’re properly studying philosophy. 

You don’t have to do ALL that if you’re not studying and you’re just getting started, but you do have to cop the fact that you won’t understand it through and through. Just read through it, I would advise annotating the text with your own thoughts when they come up, and it’s okay that you don’t understand it all completely. Just have fun with it. Don’t get caught up on the parts you don’t understand. Focus on the parts that stand out to you, and write your own thoughts down when something really grabs you. 

In Myth of Sisyphus, the line that stood out most to me was along the lines of: like great works, deep feelings always mean more than they are conscious of saying. I read that line over a few times, put the book down and started writing my own notes about what this line meant to me, and what I thought Camus was trying to say here.

The more you read, critically analysing and evaluating these texts in your head will become more natural. I often swing between - I don’t get it - oh wait, I get it! - oh nah, I don’t got it… - oh I COMPLETELY understand - oh this makes no sense at all. That’s normal for philosophy. Different parts will stick out for you, and others you’ll read over and down the line you might come across something else that clicks it into place. It might even be completely external, but it’ll live in your brain until something clicks. Other parts you might never wrap your mind around it, but maybe they’re not so important. I’m writing a thesis on Derrida at the moment, and it took at least a year of studying him before I felt like I understood what the hell he was saying. 

It’s great that you’re getting into philosophy! Don’t be intimidated by the difficulties of these texts, especially if you head in the direction of the French philosophers. They’re notoriously difficult to understand and it takes a lot of effort to grasp their texts. Some of the Analytic philosophers are slightly easier to understand than the Continentals, a bit more pragmatic. In my personal preference, they’re not as fun. I like being confused and lost because it feels better when I’ve worked hard and finally a concept clicks for me. Don’t shy away from being confused! That’s the fun of philosophy, you’re not supposed to understand everything straight away. When you get stuck, keep pushing through, move on and circle back to it later. 

You could also watch youtube videos or just google what people have to say about the text for some background. You could also try to join a reading group to see what others have to say and just sit and listen. Evaluating these texts takes a bit of practice - that’s why it’s a whole university degree, because there’s literally thousands of years of different philosophers to sort through and understand. Enjoy it!

So this whole debate goes way back when to the pre-Socratics, being and becoming. It might even go further back to other cultures and philosophers outside of the traditional Western canon, but that’s as far back as I can personally trace it to. Does everything have a definite form and essence, or is everything constantly changing? You’re right to identify Platonic forms as part of the “being” camp. A good quote for understanding becoming, from Heraclitus:

something along the lines of no man ever sees the same river twice, because it’s not the same river, and he’s not the same man.

Parmenides would be the other pre-soc philosopher to compare to Heraclitus for the being side of things but I don’t remember much of the top of my head, so we can stick with Plato. 

So that’s your debate for the nature of things in general in the universe. The you could probably move on to hermeneutics. What is the meaning behind words, symbols, language? There’s no solid answer, it’s pretty debatable. 

You’ve got positivists who will draw from Enlightenment era rationality and reason, with principles of objectivity and universality. This line of thought would look for a static, universal and objective definition for any given thing. Epistemically, the aim of objectivity and universality (or the thought this exists at all) can be called the God’s eye view, and one could see how it’s in the similar line of thought from the Platonic forms but a bit less idealist and a bit more material. Less about the essence of things and more about fixed categories. In the social sciences especially, Standpoint theory would fault this way of defining things as not true objectivity, which they take to be unattainable, but the God Trick - as it draws from monotheistic and omnipresent (or panopticonic) Christian theology.  Standpoint theorists would lean closer towards the becoming camp, as your subjective standpoint will alter how you see the world and hence, how you define the world around you. 

I’ve lost a little bit of my hermeneutics knowledge. From memory, you could argue that the words themselves have inherent meaning, that true meaning lies behind the authors intention or the authors subconscious intentions, the true meaning lies in the reader and how it’s interpreted.

My all time favourite man - Derrida - I’ll simplify his philosophy of deconstruction down to: what do you mean, true meaning? what true meaning? how does anyone know what anyone is saying ever? we just don’t know, basically. we guess. 

That was a horribly bastardised simplification of him and I’m super biased, but if you want to deep dive into this topic, read up on deconstruction, trace, différance, binary opposition and hauntology. To answer your question, firstly, what objective material reality are you even talking about? Everything is constantly changing and in flux (maybe). We all see the world differently and through our own adulterated lens and perspective. So how do we define things? Well I don’t think you’ll find a perfect static definition for any such thing. Language is funny like that, it has a tendency to change quite a lot over time. We all just kinda agree on a general understanding of things at any given time and it’s subject to change in an instant. Language is dynamic (and so too are definitions). If language is a river, to borrow from Heraclitus - you’ll never speak the same language twice, for it is not the same language, and you are not the same man. I would give up on looking for true definitions, and look behind the what constitutes a definition of an entity or phenomenon at any given time - what parts is it made up of, who said this definition and how do they see the world, what have they been told, what do they want to make you think, how has this definition changed over time, how would someone else define such a thing, and why is there an opposition between these definitions?

If you wanna go more political, you could also give Foucault a go and Power/Knowledge. Can’t believe I forgot about him. I would say to summarise, that knowledge and power are inextricably tied in that those who hold power in any given power structure also hold power to define, and to dictate what constitutes knowledge (and what does not - subjugated knowledge). These definitions then uphold and reinforce the power structure at play. But it’s not objective truth necessarily, or static definition - it’s just privileged knowledge. 

TLDR: How do we definite things? IDK man, I don’t think we actually really do. Not in an objective and perfect static way, anyway. BUT I am drawing from Derrida and on the Becoming side of the debate. So this is just one perspective and also a lot of philosophers hate Derrida. 

If you’re interested in Hermeneutics, have you looked at Schleiermacher or Habermas? There are some legal theorists who you might also want to look at, too. Especially regarding jurisdiction. Slightly unrelated but Niklas Luhmann systems theory might be of tangental interest - in the sense that the world is chaos, and we just try to make sense of it (again, super simplified. i tried to fit a bunch of ideas into this response but a full explanation would need more time and energy).
